name: Tara Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies or government. We keep your answers confidential. What does a normal shift look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I take the loader up the west bench after the pre-start check, then work with the haul trucks until handover. I like getting the flow right without rushing a dangerous load. The alarms and the paperwork can wear you down by the end of a long shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the tablet might tidy our shift sheets, but the haul trucks still need people who hear an odd engine note. Our pay is decent and the mine is busy, so I wouldn't make a drama of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be relieved. The mortgage is manageable and we've got more than six months put away, but I won't pretend a stalled promotion wouldn't sting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my usual loader shifts and check whether the new digital shift sheet misses faults. In the first year I'd put a little of each overtime payment against the mortgage, as we do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled. School shoes and the mortgage are still there, but I can see the bills getting paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exactly would you check on that sheet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare the tyre and brake notes with the machine before I sign. A tidy screen isn't the same as a sound truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything for the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My partner Rowan and I would keep their after-school swimming, because the budget already covers it.

say: I'd say **shift sheets** might get easier while operators still need to notice what a loaded truck sounds like.
I'd tell the crew the **mine** is busy enough that I see no reason to panic over a tablet.
think: I'd feel **relieved** that my skilled shifts and our mortgage payments still look steady for the next few years.
I'd still watch for a **promotion** stall, since better pay matters even with more than six months saved.
do: Keep **loader shifts** and check the machine against each digital fault sheet before signing during the first year.
Pay a little **overtime** money against the mortgage as we already do when extra shifts come through.
feel: Mostly **settled**, with ordinary school and mortgage bills still on my mind.
S0.quote: A tidy screen isn't the same as a sound truck.
fieldNote: She trusts her **ears** and hands more than a neat fault report, while accepting that simpler paperwork could save time.
Her **savings** and steady pay make the children's activities feel affordable; her private worry is a slower promotion.

steps.text: Keep loader shifts and verify each digital fault sheet against the machine
Pay overtime money against the mortgage when extra shifts come

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let the planners have their faster reports; the actual loading still needs someone in the cab for now. If robots come in slowly, I'd want the safety case shown to the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our dispatch and ordering people could lose hours before I do. I could probably move to another mine nearby, but I hate how easily a family can be told to rearrange itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the supervisor which machines are likely to be automated, then sit in on a demonstration before volunteering for anything. In the first year I'd learn the new monitoring screen if the mine installs it, and keep paying down the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, because change seems real but my own wage isn't the first one at risk. I don't enjoy being treated like a spare part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the demonstration credible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want a live run on our rough lower ramp, not a polished video from a different site. My colleague Nia knows where the wheels lose grip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mention another mine; when would you apply?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if my roster or pay actually dropped. Plenty of sites are nearby, and I would check vacancies before saying yes to a transfer.

say: I'd tell operators the **planning** desk may change quickly, while our cab work changes on a slower clock.
I'd ask for a **live run** on the lower ramp before trusting claims about driverless machines.
think: I'd worry about **dispatch** colleagues losing hours before my own roster changes, even if my household can absorb a delay.
I'd consider another nearby **mine** if my hours fall, but I dislike how a transfer could disturb family routines.
do: Ask the **supervisor** which machines are planned for automation and watch a demonstration on our actual ramp.
Learn the **monitoring screen** if installed during the first year, while continuing regular mortgage payments.
feel: **Uneasy** about colleagues and family disruption, though I still expect my wage to hold for now.
S1.quote: I'd want a live run on our rough lower ramp, not a polished video from a different site.
fieldNote: Her **test** for new equipment is a real ramp and a colleague's knowledge, consistent with adopting technology once proven.
She names a possible **transfer** but makes it conditional on actual lost hours; the planned first-year steps stay at her mine.

steps.text: Ask the supervisor for a live demonstration on the lower ramp
Learn the new monitoring screen if the mine installs one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the office side could change by 2028, but our trucks wouldn't drive themselves just because a computer can plan. The 2031 robot date is close enough that I'd ask the mine for a straight timetable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be worried our shift allocation gets squeezed before the trucks change. We have savings and other mines nearby, yet a replacement machine by 2031 could still take a big bite out of our income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the union representative and supervisor for the equipment schedule and retraining terms. In the first year after 2028 I'd train on remote equipment checks if a real course opens, and put half of overtime into the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, especially about how little time we would have between the first software changes and the machines arriving. I can still make choices, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say at home that evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Rowan that our savings buy us time, not another career. We'd postpone replacing the family car until the roster looked secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course isn't offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my loader qualification current and call two nearby mines about their operator rosters. I wouldn't pay for a vague certificate.

say: I'd point out that **planning** can change in 2028 while driverless haul trucks are a separate 2031 prospect.
I'd ask management for a **timetable** before anyone treats the current operator roster as secure or doomed.
think: I'd worry about **shift allocation** shrinking early, before robots can handle the cab work I know.
Our **savings** buy time, but a large loss of operator pay would still hit our mortgage household.
do: Request the **equipment schedule** and training terms from the supervisor and union representative before choosing a course.
Train on **remote checks** if a real course opens after 2028, and direct half of overtime against the mortgage.
feel: **Anxious** about pay and timing, with a workable cushion and nearby jobs keeping me from feeling trapped.
S2.quote: I'd tell my partner Rowan that our savings buy us time, not another career.
fieldNote: She distinguishes **software** in 2028 from possible hands-on replacement around 2031; she expects roster effects before full automation.
Training remains **conditional** on a real course, while mortgage payments and asking for equipment dates are actions she controls.

steps.text: Train on remote equipment checks if a real course opens
Pay half of overtime money against the mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say 2031 gives us years to watch the paperwork change, and 2034 is the date to worry about trucks doing the hands-on work. I would ask to see the rollout plan in plain language.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me test a new role while our children are still at school. I'm not sure remote supervision will need as many operators, so our higher pay may be the part that goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to shadow the control room for one shift this year. If they offer a recognised remote operations course, I'd take it, and after 2031 I'd review our mortgage payments against the actual roster rather than guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy now, possibly anxious if the operator roster starts thinning. The longer runway makes it easier to speak calmly at dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you ask about the control room?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my supervisor Marta for a shadow shift, because she knows the control room lead. I want to see control-room work before taking a remote operations course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would trigger a move to another mine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two rounds of fewer operator shifts would do it. I'd look at nearby mines first so the children could stay at their school.

say: I'd separate the **2031** paperwork change from the possible hands-on robot change around 2034.
I'd ask for a **rollout plan** that operators can read, with actual dates and duties rather than promises.
think: I could test **remote operations** while the children are in school, but I doubt every operator could move there.
I'd worry about losing **higher pay** even if I could keep some sort of mining job nearby.
do: Ask supervisor Marta for a **control room** shadow shift this year before paying for training.
Take a recognised **remote operations** course if offered, then review mortgage payments against the roster after 2031.
feel: **Uneasy** now because the runway allows a trial; a thinning roster would make the risk sharper.
S3.quote: I want to see control-room work before taking a remote operations course.
fieldNote: She treats a **shadow shift** as evidence, fitting her steady approach to new tools and roles.
A move stays **conditional** on two rounds of reduced shifts; keeping the children at their school is central.

steps.text: Ask supervisor Marta for a control room shadow shift
Take a recognised remote operations course if the mine offers one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a decade is enough to ask hard questions and make sensible plans. By 2036 the software could do our reports, and around 2039 robots might do the driving; those are different dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might be close to choosing lighter work by then, but I can't assume a pension will appear on the exact day machines arrive. My children will be grown, and the mortgage should be much smaller if we keep paying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working the loader and ask each year what the mine is actually buying. This year I'd raise the regular mortgage payment a little, and by 2036 I'd decide whether to apply for a safety trainer role if one exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm, though I know ten years can disappear. I can plan without pretending the mine owes me a retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much more could you pay on the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About one extra payment each year, using part of overtime rather than the children's school money. I'd stop the extra payment if our shifts fell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the mine tell operators first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the purchase dates and the number of training places, not a speech about the future. People can make decisions when the figures are real.

say: I'd say a **decade** gives operators room to ask for equipment dates and choose what to learn.
I'd distinguish **2036** report automation from possible robot driving around 2039, rather than fold them together.
think: I may prefer **lighter work** by then, but I can't count on a pension arriving with the machines.
Our **mortgage** should shrink and the children will be older if our current pay holds.
do: Keep **loader shifts** while asking the mine each year what equipment it is buying.
Make one extra **mortgage payment** this year from overtime if shifts hold, and revisit a trainer application by 2036.
feel: Fairly **calm** because there is time to plan, with uncertainty about the eventual retirement date.
S4.quote: People can make decisions when the figures are real.
fieldNote: She wants **purchase dates** and training places, rather than assurances; the decade gives room for evidence-led decisions.
Her mortgage plan uses **overtime** only and is conditional on stable shifts, protecting the children's school spending.

steps.text: Keep loader shifts and ask yearly about planned equipment purchases
Make one extra mortgage payment from overtime if shifts hold

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the paperwork could change quickly and the robot date in 2031 is too close for a casual career switch. A real equipment timetable, paid training places, and a clear operator roster would help me decide while we still have savings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to the family car and the children's school plans when people talk about jobs. A shift isn't just one person's wage; it holds a whole timetable together.

headlineQuote: A shift isn't just one person's wage; it holds a whole timetable together.
portrait: **Tara**, 43, runs mine equipment; her vocational training and higher pay support a partner, two children and a mortgage.
Her **strong savings** and nearby mines provide options, though she trusts new technology after a live test on her own rough ramp.
She moves from **calm** in AI Plateau to concern for dispatch colleagues under Steady Disruption, then worries about the short 2028-to-2031 runway.
With more **time**, she shadows the control room, considers a recognised course and pays down the mortgage from overtime when shifts hold.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** compresses the time between software changes and possible hands-on robot competition for her operator pay.
whatWouldHelp: A real **equipment timetable**, paid training places and a clear operator roster would let her plan while savings remain available.
